title: Are Consumers Myopic? Evidence from New and Used Car Purchases
research_question: How sensitive are consumers to expected future gasoline costs when making new and used car purchase decisions? Specifically, do car buyers undervalue (i.e., behave myopically toward) the future fuel costs of vehicles relative to their up-front purchase prices, given vehicles' differing fuel economies?
data_description: The primary dataset consists of individual automobile transaction records from a major market research firm covering approximately 20 percent of US new car dealerships from January 1, 1999 to June 30, 2008, including every new and used car transaction at sampled dealers. Each transaction records the exact vehicle purchased, transaction price, trade-in information, and census-block-group demographics of the buyer. A 10 percent random sample yields 1,863,403 new car and 1,096,874 used car observations. These are merged with EPA Combined Fuel Economy ratings (weighted average of highway and city MPG) for each car model and with monthly station-level retail gasoline prices from OPIS covering 15,000 Zip Codes, aggregated to 210 Nielsen Designated Market Areas. National monthly unit sales data come from Ward's Auto Infobank; vehicle survival rates and annual mileage come from NHTSA.
institutional_context: Passenger cars and light-duty trucks account for roughly 15 percent of US greenhouse gas emissions, making policy levers that influence vehicle fuel consumption central to climate policy. The main US instrument has historically been Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, but economists have proposed gasoline or carbon taxes that work by changing fuel prices. Whether such price-based instruments can shift the composition of the vehicle fleet depends on how much consumers weigh future fuel costs when buying cars. The 1999–2008 period provides substantial intertemporal variation, with national average gasoline prices ranging from about $1 to $4 per gallon, as well as cross-sectional variation across regional fuel markets driven by transportation costs, refinery margins, market power, and state-specific gasoline formulations. Consumers face a trade-off between vehicle purchase price and discounted lifetime fuel expenditures that varies sharply across fuel-economy quartiles when gasoline prices change.
